intro: Chopin’s Nocturne in E♭ major, Op. 9 No. 2, played by Patrizia Prati in November 2015 at the Museum of Romanticism in Madrid, with no audience present. The left hand keeps a steady accompaniment while the melody is repeated with added ornaments and ends in an unaccompanied flourish.

sections.label: A · Song above bass and chords
sections.mNote: Four slow beats to a bar, each divided into three.

sections.label: B · Repeated E♭s, then rising melody
sections.mNote: The bass descends through B♭, A♮ and A♭.

sections.label: C · Minor chords and rising octaves
sections.mNote: A♭-minor harmony leads to the final ascent and cadenza.

sections.label: Coda · Soft chords in E♭
sections.mNote: The first tempo returns after the free cadenza.

cues.title: Opening bar, left-hand accompaniment
cues.text: Under each slow beat the left hand plays a low note followed by two chords. Above it the melody rises from B♭ to G. Chopin marks it espressivo dolce, expressive and sweet.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), upbeat and opening bar, 12/8 and espressivo dolce. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Patrizia Prati, teachers and writing
cues.text: Prati studied piano with Giancarlo Cardini, Aldo Ciccolini and András Schiff, and harpsichord with Anna Maria Pernafelli. She has published writing on music, literature and literary translation.
cues.evidence: Patrizia Prati’s curriculum vitae, pp. 1–2, lists these teachers and her writing on literary translation: https://patriziaprati.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/Patrizia-Prati-CV-IT.pdf

cues.title: Descending bass, bars 9–10
cues.text: A new phrase starts on F, rises to G and falls back. Underneath, the bass steps down from B♭ to A♮, then A♭. The right hand repeats E♭ softly over the descent.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 9–10: F–G–F melody, descending B♭–A♮–A♭ bass and repeated E♭s. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Varied return of the opening theme
cues.text: A rapid run through G, B♭ and E♭ brings the melody back to its high G in bars 21–24, the last varied statement of the opening theme. This version has more twists, trills and accented short notes. The left hand resumes its earlier pattern under the theme.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 21–24, the last varied statement of the opening theme. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Coda over a tonic bass
cues.text: In the coda the melody is reduced to E♭, F and G. An A♭-minor chord harmonises its opening while the bass holds E♭. The melody then rises again, marked pp and sempre pp.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 25–28: Coda, tonic bass, minor-subdominant harmony, pp and sempre pp. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Cadenza, bar 32
cues.text: The bass climbs through a B♭-dominant chord and holds it. Above, the high octaves pause, then the right hand plays a four-note figure. The short cadenza is marked senza tempo, without the regular beat of the accompaniment.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bar 32: dominant arpeggio, fermata and senza tempo cadenza. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Final chords, bars 33–34
cues.text: E♭ returns in the bass beneath rocking chords, marked Tempo I. The dynamic falls from pp to ppp. The nocturne ends with three chords, and the last is held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: G. Schirmer edition (1881), bars 33–34: Tempo I, pp, ppp and final fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1590
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The bass descends beneath repeated E♭s
transitions.from: A · Song above bass and chords
transitions.to: B · Repeated E♭s, then rising melody
transitions.how: In bars 17–19 the bass steps down through B♭, A♮ and A♭ while the right hand repeats E♭. Over A♭, a major chord turns minor when C falls to C♭. The bass then reaches E♭, and the melody falls to B♭ before leaping up an octave into the next phrase.

transitions.title: A♭ minor beneath the last ascent
transitions.from: B · Repeated E♭s, then rising melody
transitions.to: C · Minor chords and rising octaves
transitions.how: A♭-minor chords return, now with A♭ itself deep in the bass. The right hand turns around E♭ and F, then climbs under the marking con forza. High octaves take over the melody and rise to the B♭ dominant chord, which is held under the cadenza.

transitions.title: Final run resolving to E♭
transitions.from: C · Minor chords and rising octaves
transitions.how: The final run descends over the held B♭ dominant seventh and ends on C and D. E♭ follows in both hands and resolves the chord. At Tempo I the first tempo returns, and the piano rolls through E♭ major, softly, before the last three chords.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
